children.text: 80C gets all the attention, but on the old regime it is only one of several deductions. The others are different in an important way: most of them reward money you are probably spending anyway, on health insurance, an education loan, a donation or a savings account. Missing them is pure loss. This lesson covers the four you are most likely to use.

stats.label: Health insurance
stats.context: Section 126 (80D), for self, family and senior citizen parents

stats.label: Education loan interest
stats.context: Section 129 (80E), for up to 8 tax years

stats.label: Donations
stats.context: Section 133 (80G), depending on where you donate

stats.label: Savings interest
stats.context: Section 153 (80TTA); ₹50,000 on deposits for senior citizens

body.text: Every deduction in this lesson works only on the old regime. On the new regime, none of them is available. They matter most when deciding whether the old regime beats the new one for you, because each of them adds to the total deductions the old regime needs to win.

children.text: Premiums for health insurance on yourself, your spouse, your dependent children and your parents qualify, in two separate buckets. Contributions to CGHS and preventive health check-ups count too. Premiums must be paid by any mode other than cash; only preventive check-ups can be paid in cash.

cells: You and parents all 60 or above

cards.definition: Up to ₹5,000 a year, included within the ₹25,000 or ₹50,000 limit, not on top. Can be paid in cash.
Medical expenses for a senior citizen who has no health insurance can be claimed within the ₹50,000 limit.
If you pay a premium covering several years in one go, the deduction is spread equally across those years.
You can claim for parents even if they are not dependent on you, as long as you pay the premium.
Premium paid by your employer does not qualify. Only premium you pay yourself, or that is deducted from your salary for a top-up you choose, counts.

body.title: Your Turn: Two Buckets
body.prompt: Pooja, 35, a teacher in Jaipur on the old regime, pays ₹18,000 for a family floater covering herself, her husband and son, plus ₹6,000 for preventive health check-ups for the family. Her parents, aged 62 and 65, have no health insurance, and she pays ₹42,000 towards their medical bills. What is her total deduction under Section 126 (80D)?
body.explanation: Self bucket: premium ₹18,000 plus preventive check-ups capped at ₹5,000 = ₹23,000, within the ₹25,000 limit. Parents' bucket: her parents are senior citizens with no insurance, so their medical expenses of ₹42,000 qualify within the ₹50,000 limit. Total = ₹23,000 + ₹42,000 = ₹65,000.

children.text: The entire interest on a loan taken for higher education is deductible, with no upper limit. The loan must be from a bank, financial institution or approved charitable institution, and must be for the higher education of yourself, your spouse, your children or a student for whom you are the legal guardian. The principal is not deductible.

events.title: Studying at IIM Indore
events.description: Loan disbursed. Interest accrues but repayment has not started, so no deduction yet.

events.title: Repayment begins
events.description: Year 1 of the deduction. The full interest she pays this year is deductible.

events.title: Seven more years
events.description: Interest paid in each year remains fully deductible.

events.title: Deduction ends
events.description: Any interest still being paid is no longer deductible, even if the loan continues.

body.label: Neha's tax saving in her first repayment year
body.context: On ₹1,05,000 of interest, at the 30% slab plus 4% cess. Because there is no cap, a large education loan can make the old regime attractive for several years after graduation.

body.title: Section 129 Check
body.question: Which of these education loans qualifies for the Section 129 (80E) deduction?
options: A loan from Varun's uncle for his engineering degree
A bank loan taken by Farida for her younger brother's MBA, where she is not his legal guardian
A bank loan taken by Mahesh for his daughter's medical degree in Russia
A personal loan used to pay for a weekend photography course
body.explanation: The loan must come from a bank, financial institution or approved charitable institution, for higher education of self, spouse, children or a student for whom you are the legal guardian. Studying abroad is allowed. A loan from a relative does not qualify, a sibling's loan qualifies only if you are the legal guardian, and a personal loan for a hobby course is not a higher education loan.

markDefs.definition: Gross total income minus other deductions under this part of the Act (such as 80C and 80D) and income taxed at special rates like long-term capital gains. Many donations are deductible only up to 10% of this figure.

children.text: Donations to approved funds and registered charities are deductible at either 100% or 50% of the amount, and some are also capped at 10% of your
. Cash donations above ₹2,000 get no deduction. You need the charity's Form 10BE certificate, and the donation should appear in your AIS.

body.caption: The four categories of Section 133 (80G) donations

cells: PM CARES Fund, Prime Minister's National Relief Fund, National Defence Fund
Jawaharlal Nehru Memorial Fund, Prime Minister's Drought Relief Fund
Donations to government or approved bodies for promoting family planning
Full amount, up to 10% of adjusted gross total income
Most registered NGOs and trusts with 80G approval, temples and religious trusts with approval
Half the amount, up to 10% of adjusted gross total income

body.caption: For donations in the most common category: 50% subject to the 10% qualifying limit.

body.title: Your Turn: The Qualifying Limit
body.prompt: Rakesh, a consultant in Kolkata on the old regime, has gross total income of ₹10,00,000 with no capital gains. He claims ₹1,50,000 under 80C and ₹25,000 under 80D. He donates ₹1,00,000 by bank transfer to a registered NGO with 80G approval (50% subject to the 10% limit). What is his Section 133 (80G) deduction?
body.explanation: Adjusted GTI = ₹10,00,000 − ₹1,50,000 − ₹25,000 = ₹8,25,000. The qualifying limit is 10% of that: ₹82,500. His ₹1,00,000 donation is capped at ₹82,500, and he gets 50% of it: ₹41,250.

body.text: A donation always costs you more than it saves in tax. Rakesh's ₹41,250 deduction saves him about ₹12,870 at the 30% slab with cess, on a ₹1,00,000 donation. Give because you believe in the cause. And be wary of anyone offering you an 80G receipt larger than what you actually donated: bogus donation claims are a common reason for tax notices.

body.title: Section 153: two versions depending on age

columns.label: Below 60 (80TTA)
points: Covers interest on savings accounts only
Banks, co-operative banks and post office savings accounts
Does not cover FD, RD or NSC interest

columns.label: 60 and above (80TTB)
points: Covers savings account interest and deposit interest
Includes fixed deposits, recurring deposits and post office deposits such as SCSS
Senior citizens claim this instead of the ₹10,000 version

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: Vivek, 34, earns ₹14,000 of savings account interest and ₹30,000 of FD interest. His deduction under Section 153 (80TTA) is ₹___.
body.explanation: Below 60, only savings account interest counts, capped at ₹10,000. His ₹4,000 of excess savings interest and all ₹30,000 of FD interest are fully taxable.

body.title: Anil, 42, finance manager in Chennai: ₹3,34,500 of deductions on the old regime
Scenario: The Missed Deductions
body.scenario: Mohan, 45, is an operations manager in Nagpur on the old regime, in the 30% slab. He has always claimed his full ₹1,50,000 under 80C and nothing else. While preparing his return, he mentions: he pays ₹32,000 for a family health policy, ₹61,000 for his parents' senior citizen health policy, ₹38,000 in interest on his son's engineering education loan (repayment started last year), ₹15,000 donated through an app to a registered NGO with 80G approval, and he earned ₹9,200 in savings account interest. His adjusted gross total income for the 80G limit is comfortably above ₹1,50,000.
body.prompt: What additional deductions can Mohan claim this year, and roughly how much tax is he saving?
body.modelAnswer: Section 126 (80D): family premium ₹32,000 capped at ₹25,000, and parents' premium ₹61,000 capped at ₹50,000, for ₹75,000. Section 129 (80E): the full ₹38,000 of interest, since the loan is for his son's higher education and he is within the 8-year window. Section 133 (80G): ₹15,000 at 50% = ₹7,500, since 10% of his adjusted gross total income exceeds ₹15,000; he needs the NGO's Form 10BE. Section 153 (80TTA): ₹9,200, within the ₹10,000 limit. Total additional deductions = ₹75,000 + ₹38,000 + ₹7,500 + ₹9,200 = ₹1,29,700. At the 30% slab plus cess, that saves about ₹40,466 a year that he has been leaving on the table. For past years, he cannot use an updated return to claim these, because updated returns can only increase tax, not reduce it. A missed deduction can be fixed only through a revised return filed before its deadline.

body.title: Documents to Collect Beyond 80C
steps: Health insurance premium receipts for your family and parents, showing the policyholder's and insured members' ages
Bills for preventive health check-ups, up to ₹5,000
Medical bills for senior citizen parents without insurance
Education loan interest certificate from your bank for the tax year
Form 10BE certificates for every 80G donation, and confirmation it appears in your AIS
Bank statements or interest certificates showing savings account interest
For senior citizens: interest certificates for FDs, RDs and SCSS

points: These deductions are available only on the old regime and add to the case for choosing it.
Section 126 (80D) allows up to ₹25,000 or ₹50,000 each for your family and your parents, with up to ₹5,000 for preventive check-ups inside those limits.
Section 129 (80E) allows all education loan interest, with no cap, for the first repayment year and the seven years after it.
Section 133 (80G) gives 100% or 50% deductions depending on the fund, often capped at 10% of adjusted gross total income, with no deduction for cash above ₹2,000.
Section 153 gives ₹10,000 on savings interest below 60 (80TTA) and ₹50,000 on all deposit interest for senior citizens (80TTB).
Most of these reward spending you already do; collect the paperwork so you never miss them.

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not tax or legal advice. Deduction limits and conditions can change with each Union Budget, and 80G eligibility depends on the recipient's approval status. Consult a qualified Chartered Accountant for decisions specific to your situation.
